options.a: Learning through senses and motor actions; object permanence develops
options.b: Concrete logical reasoning about conserved quantities such as volume and number
options.c: Symbolic pretend play and egocentric thinking before logical operations appear
options.d: Abstract hypothetical reasoning about possibilities

distractorExplanations.b: Conservation and concrete logic belong to the concrete operational stage (about ages 7–11), not the sensorimotor stage.
distractorExplanations.c: Symbolic play and egocentrism describe the preoperational stage (about ages 2–7), which follows sensorimotor.
distractorExplanations.d: Hypothetical-deductive reasoning is the formal operational stage (about age 11+), the last of Piaget's stages.

options.a: Frequent unannounced schedule changes so the student learns flexibility by exposure
options.b: Visual schedules, predictable routines, and explicit social skills instruction
options.c: Fading all visual supports early so the student relies on verbal directions
options.d: Large-group instruction without individual supports to build social exposure

distractorExplanations.a: Unpredictable changes usually raise anxiety in autism; flexibility is taught gradually with priming, not by surprise changes.
distractorExplanations.c: Visual supports are an evidence-based practice for autism; removing them early to force reliance on verbal directions undermines independence.
distractorExplanations.d: Social skills need explicit, individualized instruction; unstructured group exposure without supports does not teach the missing skills.

options.a: Academic subjects such as reading and math
options.b: IQ score alone, below about 70
options.c: One or more developmental domains
options.d: Adaptive behavior only, after age 9

distractorExplanations.a: Developmental delay covers physical, cognitive, communication, social-emotional, or adaptive domains — academic-subject deficits point to SLD.
distractorExplanations.b: An IQ cutoff plus adaptive deficits defines intellectual disability; developmental delay is defined by domain performance, not IQ alone.
distractorExplanations.d: Delay is judged across one or more domains (adaptive is just one), and the IDEA category applies through age 9, not after it.

options.a: Struggle mainly with decoding print despite typical social insight
options.b: Struggle to hold multiple steps in working memory during tasks
options.c: Struggle with gross motor planning and coordination
options.d: Struggle to understand others' perspectives and beliefs

distractorExplanations.a: Decoding difficulty with intact social insight describes dyslexia, not a theory of mind deficit.
distractorExplanations.b: Holding steps in mind is a working memory (executive function) issue, not understanding others' mental states.
distractorExplanations.c: Motor planning and coordination problems describe dyspraxia/developmental coordination disorder, not theory of mind.

options.a: Transition planning for post-school living, work, and community participation
options.b: Academic content only, since functional skills end at elementary school
options.c: Preschool readiness skills repeated until mental age matches chronological age
options.d: Vocational training that begins after the student exits school at age 22

distractorExplanations.b: Functional and life-skills instruction continues through adolescence for students with ID; it does not end in elementary school.
distractorExplanations.c: Instruction should be age-appropriate and functional; repeating preschool content based on mental age is not best practice.
distractorExplanations.d: IDEA requires transition services in the IEP by age 16 (earlier in many states); vocational preparation starts in school, not after exit.

options.a: Preschoolers ages 3 to 5 with disabilities through public schools
options.b: Infants and toddlers with disabilities or developmental delays
options.c: School-age students ages 6 to 21 with an IEP
options.d: Adults with disabilities seeking vocational rehabilitation

distractorExplanations.a: Preschool special education for ages 3–5 is IDEA Part B (Section 619); Part C covers birth to age 3.
distractorExplanations.c: School-age services with an IEP fall under IDEA Part B; Part C early intervention ends at age 3.
distractorExplanations.d: Vocational rehabilitation for adults falls under the Rehabilitation Act, not IDEA Part C.

options.a: Phonological awareness, decoding, and reading fluency
options.b: Fine motor control, visual tracking, and handwriting speed
options.c: Working memory, inhibitory control, and cognitive flexibility
options.d: Crystallized knowledge, vocabulary breadth, and general information

distractorExplanations.a: These are early literacy skills; executive functions are the self-regulation skills of working memory, inhibition, and shifting.
distractorExplanations.b: These are motor and visual-motor skills usually addressed in OT, not executive function.
distractorExplanations.d: Crystallized knowledge is accumulated learning measured on IQ subtests, not an executive control process.

options.a: Mainly affects cognitive development rather than emotional bonds
options.b: Fosters dependence that delays independent exploration
options.c: Matters mainly after the child enters formal schooling
options.d: Supports secure attachment and emotional development

distractorExplanations.a: Attachment theory centers on emotional bonds; the main described effect of responsive care is secure attachment, not cognition alone.
distractorExplanations.b: Bowlby and Ainsworth found secure attachment gives a safe base that increases exploration, not dependence.
distractorExplanations.c: Attachment forms in infancy and early childhood; the key caregiving window is well before school entry.

options.a: Inattention, hyperactivity, and/or impulsivity affecting functioning
options.b: Persistent deficits in social communication with restricted interests
options.c: Unexpected difficulty with decoding despite adequate instruction
options.d: Episodes of elevated mood alternating with depression

distractorExplanations.b: Social-communication deficits with restricted interests are the DSM-5 criteria for autism, not ADHD.
distractorExplanations.c: Unexpected decoding difficulty describes dyslexia (SLD in reading), not ADHD's attention-regulation profile.
distractorExplanations.d: Alternating mania and depression describes bipolar disorder, not ADHD.

options.a: Combine two words into short phrases like 'more milk'
options.b: Use one or few words and understand simple requests
options.c: Use about 50 words and simple two-word sentences
options.d: Coo and babble but do not yet respond to their name

distractorExplanations.a: Two-word combinations typically emerge around 18–24 months, not by 12 months.
distractorExplanations.c: A vocabulary near 50 words with word combinations is a ~24-month milestone, not a 12-month one.
distractorExplanations.d: Responding to name usually appears by 6–9 months; not responding by 12 months is a red flag, not typical.

options.a: Tasks a learner cannot complete even with expert help
options.b: Tasks a learner has already mastered independently
options.c: Tasks matched to the learner's current Piagetian stage of thinking
options.d: Tasks a learner can do with guidance but not yet independently

distractorExplanations.c: Matching tasks to a developmental stage is Piaget's framework; ZPD is Vygotsky's gap between independent and assisted performance.
distractorExplanations.a: Tasks beyond reach even with support lie outside the ZPD; they are too difficult for productive instruction.
distractorExplanations.b: Tasks already mastered independently are below the ZPD; teaching them adds little new learning.

options.a: Trisomy 21 (extra copy of chromosome 21)
options.b: A missing X chromosome in females (45,X)
options.c: A CGG repeat expansion on the X chromosome
options.d: A deletion on chromosome 15 of paternal origin

distractorExplanations.b: A 45,X karyotype (one missing X chromosome) is Turner syndrome, not Down syndrome.
distractorExplanations.c: A CGG repeat expansion in the FMR1 gene causes fragile X syndrome, not Down syndrome.
distractorExplanations.d: A paternal 15q11-q13 deletion causes Prader-Willi syndrome, not Down syndrome.

options.a: Fluent cursive handwriting and accurate spelling
options.b: Phonological awareness, letter knowledge, and vocabulary
options.c: Memorizing whole-word lists before any letter sounds
options.d: Silent reading stamina and grade-level comprehension strategies

distractorExplanations.a: Handwriting and spelling develop alongside or after early reading; they are not prerequisites for learning to read.
distractorExplanations.c: Whole-word memorization before letter-sound knowledge contradicts the science of reading; phonics builds on phonological awareness.
distractorExplanations.d: Reading stamina and comprehension strategies are outcomes of reading instruction, not prerequisite skills.

options.a: Zero-tolerance consequences applied the same way to every student
options.b: Requiring students to disclose trauma details to staff
options.c: Safety, trust, choice, collaboration, and empowerment
options.d: Reducing structure so students can self-direct freely

distractorExplanations.a: Zero-tolerance discipline ignores trauma context and can retraumatize; trauma-informed practice emphasizes safety and trust.
distractorExplanations.b: Trauma-informed practice does not require disclosure; it assumes trauma may be present and builds safety without forced retelling.
distractorExplanations.d: Predictable routines and structure increase felt safety for trauma-affected students; reducing structure works against that.

options.a: Present levels, a diagnosis code, and the teacher's lesson plans
options.b: Measurable goals, IQ scores, and the student's class schedule
options.c: Short-term objectives for every student and a behavior plan
options.d: Present levels, measurable annual goals, services, and placement

distractorExplanations.a: IEPs are not required to include a medical diagnosis code or daily lesson plans; they require measurable goals and services.
distractorExplanations.b: IQ scores belong in the evaluation report, not required IEP content, and a class schedule is not a federal IEP element.
distractorExplanations.c: Short-term objectives are required for students on alternate assessments, and a behavior plan is needed when behavior impedes learning.

options.a: Educating students with disabilities alongside nondisabled peers to maximum appropriate extent
options.b: Placing every student with an IEP in a general classroom full time with no pull-out services
options.c: Choosing the placement with the most specialized services available anywhere in the school district
options.d: Placing students in the school closest to home that has available special education openings

distractorExplanations.b: That describes full inclusion; LRE requires a continuum of placements and general education to the maximum appropriate extent.
distractorExplanations.c: LRE starts from general education with supports; choosing the most specialized setting reverses the presumption.
distractorExplanations.d: Proximity to home is a placement consideration, but LRE is about access to nondisabled peers, not seat availability.

options.a: Lower the grade-level expectations a student must meet on assignments
options.b: Change how a student accesses content without altering grade-level standards
options.c: Change what content a student learns by reducing the number of standards
options.d: Are available to students with IEPs but not to students with 504 plans

distractorExplanations.a: Lowering expectations is a modification; accommodations change access without changing what is measured.
distractorExplanations.c: Reducing the standards learned changes content, which is a modification, not an accommodation.
distractorExplanations.d: Accommodations are a core part of Section 504 plans; both IEPs and 504 plans can include them.

options.a: A schoolwide discipline matrix applied the same way to all students
options.b: The topography of the behavior as described in office referrals
options.c: Functional Behavioral Assessment identifying function of behavior
options.d: A psychiatric diagnosis identifying the student's disability category

distractorExplanations.a: A schoolwide matrix is Tier 1 PBIS; a BIP is individualized and built from the student's FBA.
distractorExplanations.b: Topography (what the behavior looks like) does not reveal why it occurs; a BIP must address the function found in an FBA.
distractorExplanations.d: A diagnosis or eligibility category does not tell you the behavior's function; the BIP is driven by FBA data.

options.a: Collected at the annual IEP review and reported once per year
options.b: Based on report card grades that combine effort and achievement
options.c: Frequent, but kept in the teacher's file rather than shared with parents
options.d: Frequent, standardized or curriculum-based, and used to adjust instruction

distractorExplanations.a: IDEA requires periodic progress reports (e.g., with report cards); once-yearly data is too infrequent to adjust instruction.
distractorExplanations.b: Grades mix effort, behavior, and achievement; IEP progress monitoring needs direct measures tied to each goal.
distractorExplanations.c: IDEA requires reporting progress on IEP goals to parents periodically; data are not kept from families.

options.a: One teach/one assist, station teaching, parallel teaching, alternative teaching, team teaching
options.b: Push-in tutoring, pull-out resource room, and self-contained class as co-teaching variants
options.c: Consultation, where the special educator advises but does not teach in the general education classroom
options.d: Paraprofessional-led instruction while the special educator plans in a separate classroom

distractorExplanations.b: Pull-out and self-contained settings are placements on the continuum, not co-teaching models where two teachers share one class.
distractorExplanations.c: Consultation is an indirect service with no shared instruction, so it is not a co-teaching model.
distractorExplanations.d: Co-teaching pairs two certified educators delivering instruction together; a paraprofessional teaching alone is not co-teaching.

options.a: Individualized modifications added after a lesson fails for a student
options.b: Multiple means of assessment, grading, and retention decisions
options.c: Multiple means of engagement, representation, and action/expression
options.d: Teaching to each student's single preferred learning style

distractorExplanations.a: UDL designs flexibility in from the start; retrofitting modifications after failure is the opposite of universal design.
distractorExplanations.b: The three UDL principles are engagement, representation, and action/expression — not assessment, grading, and retention.
distractorExplanations.d: Matching instruction to learning styles lacks research support and is not UDL, which offers multiple means to all learners.

options.a: Tutoring in academic subjects provided by a private learning center
options.b: Medical services from a physician for ongoing treatment of the disability
options.c: Surgically implanted devices such as cochlear implants and their replacement
options.d: Speech-language therapy, occupational therapy, and transportation if required

distractorExplanations.a: Related services help a student benefit from special education; private academic tutoring is not a listed related service.
distractorExplanations.b: IDEA limits medical services to diagnostic and evaluation purposes; ongoing physician treatment is excluded.
distractorExplanations.c: IDEA specifically excludes surgically implanted devices and their optimization or replacement from related services.

options.a: District proposes or refuses to change identification, evaluation, or placement
options.b: District sends a meeting invitation for the annual IEP review, before any change is proposed
options.c: Parent requests a copy of the student's education records under FERPA
options.d: Teacher adjusts daily lesson plans or seating within the current IEP

distractorExplanations.b: A meeting invitation is a meeting notice, not Prior Written Notice; PWN follows a proposal or refusal to change.
distractorExplanations.c: Records requests fall under FERPA access rights; PWN is triggered by district proposals or refusals about the IEP.
distractorExplanations.d: Routine instructional changes within the existing IEP do not require PWN; changes to identification, evaluation, placement, or FAPE do.

options.a: Assigning identical tasks and pacing so every learner gets the same opportunity
options.b: Grouping students permanently by ability level for the whole year
options.c: Adjusting content, process, product, or environment based on student need
options.d: Adjusting grades upward for students with disabilities to reflect effort

distractorExplanations.a: Identical tasks and pacing is uniform instruction; differentiation varies content, process, product, or environment by need.
distractorExplanations.b: Permanent ability tracking is not differentiation; flexible grouping changes as student data change.
distractorExplanations.d: Changing grades for effort is a grading modification, not differentiated instruction based on readiness, interest, or profile.

options.a: Disciplinary removal exceeds 5 consecutive school days in one year
options.b: A student with an IEP is suspended for any length of time for a code violation
options.c: The parent requests a reevaluation after a behavior incident
options.d: Disciplinary removal exceeds 10 consecutive days or constitutes pattern

distractorExplanations.a: The trigger is a removal of more than 10 consecutive school days (or a pattern), not 5 days.
distractorExplanations.b: Short removals of 10 days or fewer that are not a pattern do not require a manifestation determination.
distractorExplanations.c: A reevaluation request starts the evaluation process; manifestation reviews are triggered by a disciplinary change of placement.

options.a: Postsecondary education, employment, and independent living skills
options.b: Grade-level academic credits required for a standard diploma
options.c: Moving between grade levels, such as elementary to middle school
options.d: Completing guardianship paperwork and adult disability benefits applications

distractorExplanations.b: Transition services are results-oriented toward post-school outcomes, not just credit accrual for a diploma.
distractorExplanations.c: That is a grade-level transition; IDEA transition services address post-school education, employment, and independent living.
distractorExplanations.d: Guardianship and benefits may be discussed, but IDEA transition services center on postsecondary goals, not legal paperwork.

options.a: Must be provided only when a medical doctor prescribes it
options.b: Must be considered for every student with a disability
options.c: Is considered for students with physical or sensory disabilities
options.d: Is the family's responsibility to purchase for home use

distractorExplanations.a: Assistive technology need is determined by the IEP team, not by a physician's prescription.
distractorExplanations.c: IDEA requires the IEP team to consider AT for every student with an IEP, not just those with physical or sensory disabilities.
distractorExplanations.d: If the IEP team finds AT is needed for FAPE, the district provides it at no cost, including home use when required.

options.a: A predetermined mastery level for each skill
options.b: The student's own previous scores over time
options.c: A representative sample of peers (norm group)
options.d: The grade-level curriculum taught in that class

distractorExplanations.a: Comparing performance to a predetermined mastery level describes criterion-referenced testing, not norm-referenced.
distractorExplanations.b: Comparing a student with their own past scores is ipsative assessment or progress monitoring, not a norm-group comparison.
distractorExplanations.d: Measuring against the local curriculum describes curriculum-based assessment, not comparison to a norm group.

options.a: Relative standing among national peers using percentile ranks
options.b: Growth compared with the student's own earlier scores
options.c: Underlying ability through standardized cognitive subtests
options.d: Performance against a defined skill standard or criterion

distractorExplanations.a: Percentile ranks against national peers are norm-referenced scores, not criterion-referenced.
distractorExplanations.b: Comparing with the student's own prior scores is ipsative assessment, not measurement against a fixed criterion.
distractorExplanations.c: Cognitive subtests estimate ability with norm-based standard scores; criterion-referenced tests measure mastery of defined skills.

options.a: Provides a single annual score for comparison to national norms
options.b: Provides frequent, brief probes to track academic progress
options.c: Diagnoses the specific cause of a learning disability
options.d: Measures behavior function through ABC observation

distractorExplanations.a: A single annual normed score describes a norm-referenced achievement test; CBM uses frequent brief probes.
distractorExplanations.c: CBM shows response to instruction over time; it does not diagnose the cause of a disability.
distractorExplanations.d: ABC observation is part of an FBA for behavior; CBM measures academic skills such as oral reading fluency.

options.a: Using the same English-normed test for all students for consistency
options.b: Relying on nonverbal IQ scores alone to determine eligibility
options.c: Using culturally fair procedures and interpreting scores cautiously
options.d: Translating the test on the spot without checking the norms

distractorExplanations.a: Using one English-normed test for every student introduces bias for English learners; consistency is not fairness.
distractorExplanations.b: IDEA prohibits using any single measure as the sole criterion for eligibility, including a nonverbal IQ score.
distractorExplanations.d: Ad hoc translation changes the test, so the original norms no longer apply and scores become unreliable.

options.a: Achievement to classroom peers
options.b: Cognitive ability to adaptive behavior
options.c: Response to tiered interventions
options.d: Achievement to cognitive ability

distractorExplanations.a: Low achievement relative to classmates alone is not the discrepancy model, which compares achievement with measured IQ.
distractorExplanations.b: Comparing IQ with adaptive behavior is part of intellectual disability identification, not the SLD discrepancy model.
distractorExplanations.c: Response to tiered intervention is the RTI alternative to the discrepancy model, not the discrepancy model itself.

praxis-special-education-readiness-check.explanation: This item asks: “A discrepancy model for SLD identification compares”. The matching rule is: Achievement to cognitive ability (historically; many states shifting). Independent UniPrep diagnostic — not a state board exam paper. The IQ-achievement discrepancy model was the historical approach; many states now use RTI or a pattern of strengths and weaknesses instead.

options.a: Tiered increasingly intensive instruction with progress monitoring
options.b: A single cognitive test to establish an IQ-achievement gap
options.c: Grade retention for students who fail Tier 1 benchmarks
options.d: Immediate special education referral after one failed universal screening

distractorExplanations.b: An IQ-achievement gap is the discrepancy model; RTI uses tiered instruction and progress monitoring data.
distractorExplanations.c: Retention is not an RTI tier; students who miss benchmarks get more intensive Tier 2 or Tier 3 intervention.
distractorExplanations.d: RTI provides intervention and monitoring before referral; one failed screening does not trigger immediate placement.

options.a: Mastery of grade-level standards on a single untimed test
options.b: Learning potential during mediated teaching rather than static performance
options.c: A student's percentile rank compared with a national norm group at one point in time
options.d: Behavior across settings such as home, school, and community

distractorExplanations.a: A single static test of mastery is criterion-referenced assessment; dynamic assessment uses a test-teach-retest cycle.
distractorExplanations.c: Ranking against a norm group at one point is static norm-referenced testing, the opposite of dynamic assessment.
distractorExplanations.d: Gathering data across settings describes ecological assessment, not dynamic (test-teach-retest) assessment.

options.a: A standardized test administered in a quiet clinic setting
options.b: The student's performance on mediated test-teach-retest tasks
options.c: Multiple environments such as classroom, home, and community
options.d: Developmental history provided by the pediatrician alone

distractorExplanations.a: A single clinic-based standardized test removes context; ecological assessment looks at the student's real environments.
distractorExplanations.b: Test-teach-retest describes dynamic assessment, not ecological assessment across environments.
distractorExplanations.d: A medical history is one data source; ecological assessment gathers data across the student's actual environments.

options.a: Consistency of scoring across different evaluators
options.b: Consistency of scores when the same test is retaken
options.c: Consistency of items within one test measuring a trait
options.d: How well a test measures what it claims to measure

distractorExplanations.b: Consistency across repeated administrations is test-retest reliability, not inter-rater reliability.
distractorExplanations.c: Agreement among items within one test is internal consistency (e.g., Cronbach's alpha), not inter-rater reliability.
distractorExplanations.d: Measuring what a test claims to measure is validity, not reliability between raters.

options.a: Standardized achievement scores in reading and math
options.b: Antecedents, behavior, and consequences (ABC)
options.c: Cognitive ability and processing speed scores
options.d: Frequency of the behavior without its context

distractorExplanations.a: Achievement scores do not identify behavior function; an FBA collects antecedent-behavior-consequence data.
distractorExplanations.c: IQ and processing scores belong to a psychoeducational evaluation, not an FBA of behavior function.
distractorExplanations.d: Counting frequency alone omits the antecedents and consequences needed to hypothesize the behavior's function.

options.a: They are less reliable than raw scores when comparing students across ages
options.b: They can be reported only on criterion-referenced tests
options.c: They are legally prohibited in IEP eligibility reports
options.d: They imply uniform skills at an age and can mislead about scatter

distractorExplanations.a: Raw scores cannot be compared across ages at all; the problem with age equivalents is misleading interpretation.
distractorExplanations.b: Age equivalents come from norm-referenced tests; they are not a criterion-referenced metric.
distractorExplanations.c: No federal rule bans age equivalents; professional guidance discourages them because they are easily misinterpreted.

options.a: Disability discrimination by private employers with 15+ workers
options.b: Denial of an IEP to students who meet IDEA eligibility
options.c: Release of student records without parent consent
options.d: Disability discrimination in programs receiving federal funds

distractorExplanations.a: Employment discrimination by private employers is covered by ADA Title I, not Section 504's federal-funding scope.
distractorExplanations.b: IEP entitlement comes from IDEA; Section 504 is a civil rights law against discrimination in federally funded programs.
distractorExplanations.c: Unauthorized disclosure of education records is governed by FERPA, not Section 504.

options.a: Identify, locate, and evaluate children who may need special education
options.b: Evaluate children only after a parent submits a written request
options.c: Identify children enrolled in public schools but not those in private schools
options.d: Locate children ages 6 to 21 who are failing two or more classes

distractorExplanations.b: Child Find is an affirmative district duty; schools must seek out children, not wait for parent requests.
distractorExplanations.c: Child Find extends to parentally placed private school children in the district where the private school is located.
distractorExplanations.d: Child Find covers birth through 21 and any suspected disability, not just failing grades in school-age students.

options.a: Students with disabilities may be expelled without services for serious offenses
options.b: No eligible child with a disability is denied access to public education
options.c: Students are served if their disability is mild enough for general classes
options.d: Districts may decline evaluations when a child is passing all classes

distractorExplanations.a: Under IDEA, FAPE continues even during long-term disciplinary removal; zero reject means services are not cut off.
distractorExplanations.c: Zero reject covers every eligible child regardless of severity; it is not limited to mild disabilities.
distractorExplanations.d: Passing grades do not let a district refuse to evaluate a suspected disability; Child Find and zero reject still apply.

options.a: The school's grading scale and homework policy
options.b: The student's class schedule and individual teacher assignments
options.c: Rights to consent, due process, and dispute resolution
options.d: Rights to choose the specific teacher and classroom

distractorExplanations.a: Grading and homework policies are general school information, not procedural safeguards under IDEA.
distractorExplanations.b: Class schedules are not procedural safeguards; the notice explains consent, due process, and dispute rights.
distractorExplanations.d: IDEA gives parents the right to participate in placement decisions, not to choose the specific teacher or classroom.

options.a: Parents disagree with a teacher's grade on a single assignment
options.b: A student disagrees with a schoolwide dress code rule
options.c: Parents want a different general education teacher assigned to the child's class
options.d: Parents and district disagree on identification, evaluation, placement, or FAPE

distractorExplanations.a: Individual grading disputes are not due process issues; hearings address identification, evaluation, placement, or FAPE.
distractorExplanations.b: General school rules that apply to all students are not IDEA due process matters.
distractorExplanations.c: Teacher assignment is an administrative decision, not a dispute over identification, evaluation, placement, or FAPE.

options.a: Established the right to a free appropriate public education
options.b: Declared separate educational facilities inherently unequal
options.c: Required states to evaluate children with disabilities at no cost
options.d: Defined the 'some educational benefit' standard for an IEP

distractorExplanations.a: FAPE was established by PL 94-142 (1975), not Brown v. Board of Education (1954).
distractorExplanations.c: Free evaluation requirements came from PL 94-142/IDEA, not Brown, which addressed racial segregation in schools.
distractorExplanations.d: The 'some educational benefit' standard came from Board v. Rowley (1982), later raised by Endrew F. (2017).

options.a: Disability civil rights in employment and public places
options.b: Protection of student record privacy for families
options.c: Right to education for children with disabilities
options.d: Early intervention services for infants and toddlers

distractorExplanations.a: Employment and public accommodation protections come from the ADA (1990), not PL 94-142.
distractorExplanations.b: Student record privacy comes from FERPA (1974), not PL 94-142.
distractorExplanations.d: Infant and toddler early intervention (now Part C) was added by the 1986 amendments (PL 99-457), not the 1975 law.

praxis-special-education-readiness-check.explanation: This item asks: “PL 94-142 (1975) established”. The matching rule is: Right to education for children with disabilities (precursor to IDEA). Independent UniPrep diagnostic — not a state board exam paper. PL 94-142, the Education for All Handicapped Children Act, is the precursor to IDEA.

options.a: Records may be shared with any district employee who requests them
options.b: Parents may view records only after the student turns 18
options.c: Directory information requires written consent each time it is released
options.d: Personally identifiable information is protected with limited disclosure

distractorExplanations.a: FERPA allows access by school officials with a legitimate educational interest, not any employee who asks.
distractorExplanations.b: Parents hold FERPA rights until the student turns 18; at 18 the rights transfer to the student.
distractorExplanations.c: Directory information may be released without consent if the school gave annual notice and a chance to opt out.

options.a: Maintaining competence, confidentiality, and advocating for students
options.b: Sharing a student's diagnosis with classmates to build understanding
options.c: Deferring to administrators even when services in the IEP are not delivered
options.d: Using physical restraint as a first response to disruptive behavior

distractorExplanations.b: Disclosing a disability to peers without consent breaches confidentiality under CEC ethics and FERPA.
distractorExplanations.c: CEC ethics require advocating for students when IEP services are not provided, not silent deference.
distractorExplanations.d: Restraint is a last resort for imminent danger, used by trained staff — not a first response to disruption.

options.a: Testing in English first so the scores can be compared with national norms
options.b: Using a family member as interpreter to save time during formal testing
options.c: Assessments in native language when feasible and nondiscriminatory tools
options.d: Delaying evaluation until the student is fully proficient in English

distractorExplanations.a: IDEA requires assessment in the child's native language when feasible; English-first testing confounds language and disability.
distractorExplanations.b: Untrained family interpreters compromise validity; trained interpreters and appropriate tools are needed.
distractorExplanations.d: Districts cannot delay evaluation for English proficiency; Child Find requires timely, nondiscriminatory evaluation.

options.a: Binding arbitration that parents must accept before a hearing
options.b: A required step parents must complete before filing due process
options.c: A hearing before an impartial officer who issues a written decision
options.d: Voluntary facilitated negotiation before or instead of due process

distractorExplanations.a: IDEA mediation is voluntary and nonbinding unless an agreement is signed; it is not mandatory arbitration.
distractorExplanations.b: Mediation is voluntary; the resolution session, not mediation, is the step that normally follows a due process complaint.
distractorExplanations.c: An impartial hearing officer issuing a decision describes a due process hearing, not mediation.
